utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Josse, are you ready to continue the examination of Mr. Maricic?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It was the 16th of May of 1992 that you, Mr. Maricic, was severely wounded in the course of the armed conflict that this Tribunal is dealing with; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Very briefly, how were you injured and what was the nature of your injuries?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at the front line in the area of Brcko known as Ivici. At one moment our line was attacked by both Muslim and Croat forces. They were so close that I got hit by a burst of fire from an automatic rifle. I had a fracture of my upper leg and a fracture of my right hip and I was hospitalised. I was treated for those wounds at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The hospital that you -- where you were treated was in Belgrade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How did you get to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was taken there by an old ambulance vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How long were you in hospital for?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed in Belgrade for 72 days, and then I was transferred to Banja Koviljaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And that's a spa town; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you eventually returned to Brcko in September of 1992?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you remember the date that you returned to Brcko, the exact date?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't, but it could have been sometime around 10th to 12th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why did you return to Brcko?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I returned because I hail from Bukvik, and there were rumours that Bukvik would be attacked, and that's why I returned, to help if I could in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, forgive me, Mr. Josse, if I interrupt you, but in a situation like this where you were wounded whilst fighting, could you tell us whether heavy weapons were used in this fighting, or were people using machine-guns, or guns? What kind of war was it? Were people using cannons? Were -- was there any bombing? Do you understand my question? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There were -- there was no heavy weaponry, only light arms, rifles and an occasional machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the learned Judge's questions, it might help if you were to briefly describe how regularly you were involved in the sort of combat that -- again, let me rephrase this. How often you personally saw action that was similar to the type of action that took place on the day that you were badly injured?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that this was the only real fight that I participated in. Everything before that was just moving the line forward. The enemy would withdraw. That's why I did not have an opportunity to participate in any serious fighting, save for that one time when I was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Are you able to comment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be a -- and it's when your microphone is open. I don't know whether it is -- yes, now it's -- could one of the technicians have a look at what happens if Mr. Josse opens his ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I know the interpreters won't hear this. The microphone is off.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We can't hear the counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could someone assist, because if Mr. Josse opens his microphone, then we get a -- it's still there. The technicians will come and assist you. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: For some reason it's Mr. Karganovic's computer. He'll do without for now. When I say his computer, the computer he is using. It's the Court's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's always those who are working are blamed for causing problems. Mr. Josse, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As far as you could judge and see in the fighting that you were involved in, Mr. Maricic, were the weapons on both sides of similar capacity and capability? If you can't comment, say so.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the enemy, i.e., the Muslims and the Croats, had somewhat better weapons. They had machine-guns, for example, and on our side, on the line where I was, we did not have a single machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I'd like to ask the witness. How far were you able to observe the weaponry? I mean, had you any knowledge beyond what you could see yourself? I mean, I take it you had a view of perhaps a couple of hundred metres. Would you have information about what happened at a greater distance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand your question well, we had a very close encounter, and I believe the enemy could not have been more than a hundred metres away during that attack. They sneaked up on us and they attacked us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I would like to know if you say they had slightly better weapons whether -- how limited your knowledge was. Were you aware of what happened in your immediate neighbourhood, or did you have information from further away, let's say what you could not see or hear yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have information as to what kind of weapons they had at a larger distance. I only know when we came head to head that they had better weapons than we did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you said whether they had -- what weapons they had at a distance. Are you aware of what weapons you had at a distance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the unit where I was, there was no heavy weaponry. The heaviest pieces of equipment we had were a couple of machine-guns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's true for at a distance as well, what you could not see, other parts of town or other parts of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I can't confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Judge Hanoteau.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have another question to put to you. Witness, on the day you were wounded, the 16th of May, not only on that day but the days before that, were you able to see any soldiers, army soldiers, a great number of army soldiers? Were you able to see any tanks or artillery weapons in Brcko, whether it be -- whether it be on the Serb side, Muslim side, or Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that at the beginning the Serb side had more artillery. I heard detonations coming from the Serb side. Later on, that ratio changed, and towards the end of the war there was an even situation. I personally did not see any heavy weaponry, any tanks. I might have seen one tank, a single tank, but I'm not sure of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you did say that this artillery was on the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not all. I heard fire being opened, and I believe that detonations were on the enemy's side. And at the same time there were detonations on the Serb side as well, but not to such a large extent and not from such large-calibre weaponry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you stand by the fact, as you said yesterday, that the JNA was there but there weren't very many JNA soldiers there during this period, i.e., between the months of April and May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I this I that that may be the case. This is the information that I have. I can't speak of the things that I didn't see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you yourself, you didn't see a single JNA soldier, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a state of confusion. There may have been some. I personally didn't see them, not on the part of the line where I was. They were not members of the command cadre. They were not on the strength of the unit. I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said yesterday that you belonged to the -- one of the three fighting squads; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Three companies, which is a somewhat larger unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were these men wearing uniforms, and were you yourself wearing a uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those were members of the Territorial Defence, and some of the men wore their civilian clothes, trainers on their feet. They looked rather colourful. I was fortunate or unfortunate enough to get hold of a proper uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were these uniforms different from the JNA uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mostly those were the old JNA uniforms that were obsolete, that were no longer used. And those uniforms were mostly distributed amongst the members of the Territorial Defence or the civilian protection. The regular JNA troops no longer wore those at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I can inform Your Honours that the next witness who comes from a completely different part of the war, so to speak, different area, he can give evidence as to combat activities to a far greater degree than this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What physical condition were you in when you returned in the middle of September to Brcko?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had not fully recovered. I used crutches to walk, and I felt really weak.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could the witness have the large coloured map, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, would you please assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm grateful to Mr. Registrar. 151, D151. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Perhaps, first of all, using the pointer you would indicate the predicament that you understood the Serb population of Bukvik to be in, in the middle of September.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Using the pointer initially, in due course I think I'll ask you to actually mark this on the plan in black pen, could you indicate the situation that you understood the population of Bukvik to find themselves in, in September of 1992? Put another way, Mr. Maricic, why were they in difficulty?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then I don't have to show anything. Bukvik is the area on one side of which there is a series of Muslim settlements, and on the other side there is a chain of Croat settlements. The area of Vukovic is inhabited only by the Serbs. On both sides the area was encircled or surrounded by either Croats or Muslims, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How did you become aware of this information, bearing in mind you weren't there.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was born in Bukvik. I know every hamlet there. I worked as a market inspector in Brcko municipality. For a few years I was always travelling, and geography is something that I am very fond of. I like to travel. So I know everything in the entire area of Brcko and particularly in Bukvik.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Perhaps it's my fault for not making my question clear enough, Mr. Maricic, but in September of 1992, we know two things. First of all, you were quite severely incapacitated. Secondly, you were in Brcko. You weren't in Bukvik. You became aware that the Serbs of Bukvik were in real difficulty. How did you become aware of that? What was your sources of information? That's really what I'm driving at in the question I just asked.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I understood while the war was going on, and I knew that even before the war, that Bukvik as an area -- will find itself in a very serious situation. I tried to persuade my family to send women and children outside. They didn't do that. The situation worsened, and when I was in hospital in Belgrade, I followed the news, read the newspapers, and I had the impression that Bukvik would be attacked. It was already encircled. Autumn and winter were coming, and Muslims needed a corridor to Tuzla, and that corridor would have to go through Bukvik, so it would be attacked. Furthermore, I knew that Bukvik is without weapons, without men, without defence capacity. And that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I would like you to draw, if you can, on the map the encirclement that you have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bukvik you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You used the words "it was already encircled." No one -- I'm not holding you to an absolutely accurate portrayal of the encirclement, but so that the Chamber has some idea where enemy forces were in relation to the population of Bukvik. Only do this if you can help.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I will be able to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As we -- as we look at the map, which forces were to the left of the line that is on -- that you have just drawn that is on the left-hand side of the map? The left-hand side. Other side. Which forces were the other side of that line?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the other side of that line was the 108th HVO Brigade, which included both Croats and Muslims. However, half of the settlements on this side were Croats, and on the other side there were Muslims, Muslim settlements. On this side there were more Muslims, so they also held part of the Croat line on this side.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This may seem a stupid question, but based on the map that you have drawn, why was it impossible - perhaps it wasn't impossible - for the population of Bukvik to escape to Brcko?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. To run away from Brcko or to run away to Brcko?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: To Brcko from Bukvik. You've described how the population of your hometown was surrounded. Why weren't they able to go to Brcko, which was controlled by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, quite simply enemy forces of the Muslims and Croats would not let them. They were completely encircled. I don't know if I managed to show it here. They were completely encircled, and they had no capacity even to defend themselves let alone break through enemy lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Are you able to draw the encirclement at the north end of the map? Only do it if there was a physical encirclement.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it absolutely did exist. This is it, approximately. Let me just add that Ulica village, which is here in the north, I drew it on this line, it was a strongly Croat village, and it was held by Croats and Muslims, whereas this hamlet, Purici, here, which was where the line went approximately. I'm sorry I couldn't draw it more accurately. I'm not a good draftsman.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Very well. That's helpful. Thank you. Well, tell us what happened to these Serb villages in the Bukvik area at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time of the attack?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my estimate that Muslims and Croats had wrongly assessed the situation of Bukvik and its arms supply. They thought Bukvik was well organised and well equipped. That's the information I got after the war. So they had brought reinforcements from other brigades apart from the 108th brigade, and from absolutely all sides they attacked the area. In my view, this area did not need even a third of the forces used. When they finally entered Bukvik, they started looking for tanks and cannons, and there absolutely weren't any.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When did this attack take place?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the 14th of September, 1992. I think around 1400 hours, but I can't be sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your -- I'm going to ask you some questions. Not very many, a few about the attack and about its consequences. What are your sources of information as to what happened, bearing in mind you weren't there.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am certainly informed. Many of my family members died there. My nearest and dearest were there, and when it was all over, when they were captured and when they were later released after a year or so from a Muslim Croat prison in Tuzla, they told me the whole story in great detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, for the purposes of my questions, I don't think we need it in great detail, but tell us in broad outline what happened.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said the attack started from all sides, a very strong attack. That whole area including 13 villages and hamlets was very poorly equipped and even more poorly organised. There was no defence to speak of. Panic started immediately. Whereas the Muslim and Croat forces were regular forces, and they knew how to spread panic among civilian population. They burnt the first houses they came across, and the Muslim part of the forces were crying out, "Allahu Akbar." The people got very frightened. And they killed all those who -- whom they captured by the night of that day, around 150 men, women, and children, including the elderly and the sick.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you've said that prisoners were taken to Tuzla. Were they taken to Tuzla immediately?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm going to say now is very important to my whole testimony and to Brcko. In the area of Brcko there was one collection camp, Luka, whereas on the Muslim Croat side of the Brcko municipality I know there were at least five such camps, and all that population was first taken to those camps. If you want me to show them on the map I can. And after a lot of abuse and rape of women and girls they started a selection, a triage. Some members of the SDS, let's say, or those who took part in the defence were sent to one place, whereas the others were distributed across the camps in the territory of Brcko municipality. Some of their soldiers were later tried after the war on charges of rape, but they got minimal sentences. I don't know if you want me to show you the camps for Serbs on the map, but this is a fact, something you can't hide.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. If you could be given the map and the pen that would help, thank you.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll start from the north side.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could the witness have a pen, please. It would be more helpful simply to mark with a -- perhaps with a cross, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first camp, a large one holding hundreds of captives was in the village called Ulica. It used to be a modern Croat village.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object as to the relevance of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have not stopped you, Mr. Josse, although the question came into my mind as well. Say the following, that -- I don't know whether it's disputed by the Prosecution that camps, detention, abuse, ill-treatment, killing happened at the other side as well. Is that in dispute?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It is not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, it seems -- I did not stop you because I could imagine that it's important for the Defence to demonstrate what the fears and perhaps the right fears of the people were at that time that they became true. Then of course the question is whether if we hear that five camps were there holding a lot of detainees what it adds in this respect to know exactly where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I understand. Your Honour is saying the detail doesn't matter, and at this moment I'm not going to argue with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I've virtually finished on this topic. Could I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We have some photographs that we'd like to circulate from a book, and perhaps I could just deal with that in conclusion on this issue. Parts of this may need to be sent for translation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Maricic, you have brought a book with you to The Hague. It is called "Dossier Brcko"; is that correct? That there are other copies. It would help if they went into the interpreters' booths. I'm sorry. Mr. Maricic, it's very important that you answer my questions here because I want to deal with this speedily and concisely. You have brought a book to The Hague called "Dossier Brcko." That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The book is written by someone called Izica [sic] Simic.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ilija Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry. I can't read someone's handwriting. And the book contained lists of those killed and injuries in the instances you've just described, and also some photographs. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And these are some of the photographs. Could we go to the very first photograph, please. It shows a church, and this is Church of Saint Elijah in Bukvik. It says it was demolished in 1992 during combat operations. It says, "Interior destroyed." And I'm sure I can lead on this. Basically, your information is that this church was torched; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I went inside, and I saw that everything was burnt.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And we see some graffiti on the wall of the church. Perhaps the witness could be given the original photograph from the book, please because I think that would help. I'd like you to read out what the graffiti says.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is more visible on this copy than in the book, but the letters are the same. "Zmaj," or Dragon of Bosnia, and other graffiti testified that this is vandalism by Muslim soldiers, and I went inside and I saw that there were many other militant symbols and iconography, similar inscriptions mainly by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: All right. Let's go through this very quickly, please. Give the book back to Madam Usher?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see, Mr. Josse, that there is a -- SDA is written on it as well. Could we explore the context of where SDA appears? It seems to be right after the door, the side door of the church. Do you see that, Mr. Maricic? Otherwise, we could perhaps ask even the assistance of the interpreters whether it's legible at all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot show you that. I don't want to guess or maybe things up, and I don't find it legible enough. Or, rather, yes, yes, it is written along the vertical line. Yes, right of the door, in large letters, SDA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but SDA is not only the text there. Can you read what we find around SDA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't make that out. I think those are names, but I can't make them out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I'm asking that because if SDA appears there to could be in the context of the "SDA greets you," or it could be "SDA to hell." You understand what I mean? It's -- I'm trying to interpret what we see here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I -- Your Honour's asking -- yes, I do follow exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you could clarify the issue or perhaps even if that would take on the next break, but I'd like to -- I'd like know the context. So, therefore, if you could clarify that. I can imagine that it will take you some time. And also, we might have to interpret this. My colleague says that it's not written in Cyrillic, which could also mean something. But at least could we read what it says on the bottom of --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I say -- I don't want to give evidence, but in the photograph in the book it's far clearer. Of course it's smaller, so what I'm going to try and have done is have this photograph blown up in a clearer way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it's relevant. Of course, if -- if it just confirms, then I'll accept that. And could we read what is written below? Could you, Mr. Maricic, could you please slowly read the title under photograph 14.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see the number 14, but below the word Zmaj it says Muamed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Whatever you can read that's on the wall. As a matter of fact, I was referring to the title underneath the photograph, but whatever you can read from the photograph, from what's written apart from the word Zmaj, please tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, the name that is rather well known, Zmaj, or Dragan of Bosnia, and that was the name of a Turkish military leader who was a native of Gradacac who is Husein Pasa Kapetanovic who used to lead Bosnian Muslims in the resistance movement to the reform of the Ottoman Empire led by Mustafa Kemal Atatürk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to tell us the whole of the history but rather to read what we can see. You say it says Muamed. I can see that. There seems to be something like --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Muamed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- or -- okay. Mr. Josse, you'll certainly have an opportunity during the break to -- Could you please read what's written underneath the photograph? It says 14, and then ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this is clearly legible. It says "Church of the Saint Prophet Ilija in Bukvik, destroyed outside of war operations in 1992 with the inventory destroyed."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which raises more questions than outside the war to mean at another movement and not part of combat activities. It's not entirely clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What do you understand the author to mean when he used the expression "Outside of war --"

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm going to object to an interpretation of Mr. Josse of an author. The text speaks for itself. If there is other text that can refer or clarify, then that should be referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it what we just said about the detention facilities also on the basis of the evidence we already received, it's not the Prosecution case that no churches were destroyed even outside combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Next photograph, please, Mr. Maricic. Number 15. I

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Next photograph, please, Mr. Maricic. Number 15. I think you'll need your reading glasses. Could you read the caption.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The interior of the church in Bukvik as it appears now."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you mentioned that you have been there. When was the first time you went there after the war? Or during the war, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't go there during the war, and after the war I must say I wasn't in a great hurry to go there because I knew there wasn't much to see. So it was maybe a year after the war, maybe even more, that I visited the church again, and it was in this same state.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Number 16. Am I right that the caption basically says "Heavily damaged fresco of Saint Sava in Bukvik church?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: 17, please. This is the burial of 36 victims from Bukvik at Brcko cemetery on August the 21st, 1998? Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's right you attended this funeral?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And, basically, when is it thought or known that the people who were being buried on August the 21st, 1998, had died?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the people who were buried on that occasion had been killed in Bukvik on the 14th of September or maybe a day or so later, maybe one day later, actually, during this attack on the area of Bukvik.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And finally number 18. I -- is in fact a lady at the grave of her brother who it says was murdered while wounded in Donji Bukvik, and it names the lady and her brother; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says here, and I believe that it is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm in Your Honour's and the registrar's hands as to the numbering of the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: At that will be D152, Your Honours, from A to E. Five photographers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What's happened -- two things. Firstly, I'm sure I can lead on this, various members of your extended family were killed during the course of the attack that you have just mentioned; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Secondly, what has happened to your family land in Bukvik following this incident and the war?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything was a hundred per cent destroyed. Everything was torched. Whatever did not burn to the ground they took away. So all that remains now is empty land. Absolutely everything. Not a single house in the 13 hamlets remains. The cultural centre, the school. All the houses, save for one, in the former centre of Bukvik remains intact because this is where very early on the Muslim-Croat forces billeted their police.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to move on to short, discrete, and completely different topics. You have told the Chamber that you were an SDS activist back in 1991. I want to ask you about this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, from a distance I see it's the 19th of December document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: With the A and B variants.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's absolutely right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You've had a chance to look at it recently, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you see it in 1991 or 1992?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw this document for the first time a few days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And having considered or having read its contents, were you aware of its contents in the early part of 1992, in the months before the war?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A couple of days ago, I was provided with this document, and this is where I read it and learned of its contents. Before that, I didn't know anything about this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I also want to ask you about something called the six strategic goals. Do you have any awareness of that as a doctrine or mantra of the SDS in 1992?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of these six strategic goals I didn't know anything. The first time I'm hearing about those strategic goals is now. Whether there were three of them or six of them, I didn't know anything about them before.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll have that document back, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yesterday, you gave evidence about your knowledge of Mr. Krajisnik in 1991. Do you have any information or knowledge about him coming to Brcko in 1992?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have this information, and personally I don't think he ever came to Brcko. If he had, I don't know anything about it. However, since I had time on my hands and I wasn't short of money, I moved around, and if he had come to Brcko, I would have learnt about that. As far as I know, Mr. Krajisnik did not move about too much.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What do you say to the suggestion that the SDS inspired the presence and use of paramilitaries in Brcko in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only do I think, but I believe that the democratic party did not have anything to do with the paramilitaries. As I've already told you, I believe I told you yesterday, this was beyond the Serbian Democratic Party, especially when the war operations started. Nobody ever asked that party anything. The president of that party suffered himself at the hands of some members of those paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what do you say to the suggestion that events in Brcko were being controlled by the SDS leadership in Pale? In -- I should make this clear. At the time of the outbreak of the war, they were inspiring and/or condoning the activities of all concerned in Brcko on the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't claim that there weren't certain moves. However, I think, as I said here, that Brcko was to a certain extent neglected by everybody, because it had a lower percentage of the Serbian population, and I suppose that the reckoning was that it was very unlikely that it could be defended and that's why so little attention was paid to it. I am not saying that there were no such activities. However, I didn't notice any large-scale activity, although I was in a position to notice them had there been any.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You've begun the last answer by saying, "I can't claim that there weren't certain moves." What do you mean by "certain moves," please?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose some of this did exist. I don't remember any details. However, Dr. Beli was a member of the Main Board and the president of the Municipal Board of the SDS, and he was a very strong personality on the eve of the war at a general level. I'm sure that he had contacts. I'm sure that he had them. It would have been unlikely if -- for him not to have had any contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: For the avoidance of any doubt, what do you say about the proposition that the local SDS, of which you were vice-president, was controlling events in Brcko in April and May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said it. The SDS was completely pushed aside on the eve of the war and at the beginning of war operations. Dr. Beli, president of the SDS, did not serve in the army, but that is not the main reason. The main reason is that the said SDS was a right-wing party, and the key positions were held by those people who were on the left wing, first in the JNA and then in the Territorial Defence. Maybe this will sound a bit far-fetched for me to say this, but in Brcko the main roles are played by the leftists, somewhat disguised but certainly former communists and yes-men who are prepared to obey the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm very nearly finished. You've just used the phrase "are played by the leftists." Do you mean now or at the time?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time there was a League of Communists and Socialist Party and different leftist forces who held strings in their hands, and now they have formed the so-called Socialist Party, the SDP, but they're still communists, under a different name. And maybe because there are yes-men, the representatives of the international community nowadays accept them. There is probably a lot of money involved in that. I suppose they've all found their interests. So I'm talking about the present time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I have one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Again for the avoidance of any doubt, the leftist local elements whom you have just described, to what extent were they under the influence in the spring of 1992 of the SDS leadership in Sarajevo or Pale?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No influence at all. The SDS did not have any influence on the left-wing elements, if I understood your question well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I put one clarifying question. Could you tell us when War Presidency was established in Brcko, who were members of that War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the instructions that I received, everything that I was supposed to do in other towns, what Serbs were supposed to do, did not penetrate Brcko easily. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked: When a war Presidency was established in Brcko, who were members of that War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know when it was founded. I don't know who its members were. That was what I was going to say, because it was not firmly organised. There may have been a president and one or two members, but I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My following question: You are quite pertinent in your answers saying that the SDS was not controlling events. At the same time, you now tell us that did not know who were members of that War Presidency, which leaves it open that it could be leftists or SDS members or whatever. So I'm -- I'm wondering how to interpret your answers and how to assess your level of knowledge in this respect. If you could assist me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that you're right when you say that the leftists also may have been members of the War Presidency, because it was not just the SDS that decided on the establishment of -- of the War Presidency. However, the list of members was never put in front of me, and I'm not aware of its composition at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said it was not just the SDS that decided on the establishment of the War Presidency. Could you tell us what you know, then, if it's not just the SDS? Who, then, would have decided on the establishment of the War Presidency, and what do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not challenge the possibility that the SDS may have been behind the establishment of the SDS [as interpreted], but I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that you wanted to say, "may have been behind the establishment of the War Presidency." It appears here as the establishment of the SDS. So do I understand your testimony correctly if you say, "I have no knowledge on the way and the level the SDS was involved in establishing and the functioning of the War Presidency," is this a right understanding? If not, please correct me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that you understood my testimony well. I have practically no knowledge on -- on the establishment of the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for those answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I've got some follow-up questions, if I may, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The -- you haven't dealt with it because I haven't asked you, but the municipality of Brcko was divided on ethnic lines before the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't divided. I wouldn't put it that way. In any case, not officially.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How would you put it, please?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were areas where the majority Serb population and also areas where the majority Muslim population, and likewise areas with a majority Croat population, but no lines could be drawn even on a map in order to separate those areas. They were very mixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, this is clearly quite a large topic and not one that personally I'm going to ask you about, but to what extent were the SDS involved in the decision to do this and the administration of this division?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a conversation with the SDA and the HDZ, the SDS proposed the municipality of Brcko should be split amongst the three peoples. The SDS did their utmost to avoid a war, maybe because they were the weakest in the municipality. However, the other two sides did not accept that proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And are you able to assist the Chamber as to why the SDS proposed that the municipality should be split amongst the three peoples?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SDS had the interest of the Serb people in mind. They wanted to save the Serb people. War was imminent, Brcko was somewhat isolated, and a variant was sought even if it was a division, all to avoid a conflict, a war. And I believe that this was the only reason why the SDS asked for such a division.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I have nothing else on the topic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Harmon, perhaps it might be a good idea that we start cross-examination after the break. We would have seven minutes left only. Mr. Maricic, we'll have a break, 27 minutes. We'll restart at ten minutes to eleven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, before you start your cross-examination, I would like to deal with two procedural issues. I'll start with the second one, Madam Usher, but of course I'll start with the first one first, then you may already try to find the witness. The first one is a statement on Assembly and Presidency sessions and on P64A. The Trial Chamber would like to address the Prosecution regarding the records of the Bosnian Serb Presidency and the Bosnian Serb Assembly already submitted. In reviewing these documents, the Chamber has noted some gaps. The Chamber would like to request the Prosecution to look for and submit the full records of the 15th, the 20th, and the 21st sessions of the Bosnian Serb Assembly. Part of the record of the 20th session and the minutes of the 21st session are already in evidence. The Chamber notes that the Treanor report states that there are no full records available for the 15th and the 21st sessions. However, these documents might have been found in the meantime, or investigators from the Office of the Prosecution or investigators from the Defence team might be able to retrieve them. The Chamber also notes that it has not received at least one record of a Bosnian Serb Presidency session, that is the 16th session. It might also be that other unnumbered sessions were not tendered into evidence. The Chamber therefore asks the Prosecution to provide all of the available records of the Bosnian Serb Presidency which took place in 1992 in a single binder. To be clear, this binder should include the records of the sessions already in evidence, as well as the record of the 16th session and of other sessions not tendered thus far. The tabs of the binder should clearly indicate the items already in evidence and the new items that will need to be considered for admission. The Chamber asks the Prosecution toll submit these documents as soon as possible or at the latest by Friday, the 7th of April. In addition to the above, the Chamber wishes to address a related matter. The registrar, upon instructions of the Chamber, will re-number each tab contained in the 28 binders comprising Exhibit P64A. That is the footnote to the Treanor report. This is necessary in the process of scanning these documents to make them accessible electronically through the judicial database. Once the registrar completes this task, all parties will be provided with the information through the exhibit list, which will reflect the descriptions and tab numbers of all tabs contained in P64A. At that point, the Prosecution is asked to provide a concordance table containing, for each document in P64A, the new tab number, the old tab number, the ERN numbers of the English and the B/C/S versions of the document in question, and, when a document is already in evidence, the other exhibit numbers relating to the document. In this way, it will be possible for the parties, the Chamber, and any interested person to retrieve and cite more easily the documents contained in P64A. One reason for the Chambers earlier request to the Prosecution for a binder containing the records of all Presidency sessions is the difficulty we face in navigating and citing items comprising P64A. This concludes the Chamber's request and announcement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't want to get difficult about this, but could I make this observation: Personally I have not been involved in what I'm about to state, but other members of our team have been heavily involved in trying to put together these documents for the purposes of Mr. Krajisnik's proposed testimony. A great deal of time and effort has gone into that, and it would have helped, with respect, if we had had some advanced notice that the Chamber had this in mind, because realistically I need to liaise with Mr. Stewart and, in particular, the junior member of our team who has spent literally weeks on this particular task to find out if what the Chamber has now ordered will alter the considerable work that has already been done. Personally, I have no idea, frankly, Your Honour. I'm glad to say I haven't been involved in it, but others have. And had there been some liaison that this was in the pipeline, then we could have made some representations about it. I could have spoken to those in our team who have been working on this particular project, and we could have had some input into what I might otherwise say, with respect, seems a very sensible and good idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, it might be -- if this would have been in the pipeline already for a long time, the Chamber would certainly have announced that. You may have noticed that, especially during recent sessions, that the struggle you describe your team member had was most likely the same struggle as the Chamber had. So therefore it -- the Chamber wanted to resolve these matters. The Chamber would not have opposed any suggestion by the Defence to say this is so disorganised, could a solution be found, could the Chamber order the establishment of a concordance table or another organising. So what you're addressing the Chamber I'm in return addressing the Defence if you may have noticed on these practical matters that the Chamber always tried to accommodate and facilitate the Defence. But perhaps before Mr. Harmon starts selecting all the material this afternoon, perhaps if you would have any further suggestions which, after you have shown the state I have just given to your team member, if that would -- if he would say, well, if you change this then it's less work for the Prosecution and it works better, then, of course, I take it, Mr. Harmon, you would wait until tomorrow before starting.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is exactly I was going to suggest. If we could have 24 hours before the request or order that has just been made is executed by the Prosecution that would help enormously. I'm going to e-mail this to the relevant members of our team immediately. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Usher, I start now the second matter. The Trial Chamber, Mr. Josse, and I'm now mainly addressing the Defence, we'd like to address the third and the fourth requests for guidance filed by the Defence on the 17th and the 20th of March, 2006, respectively. The Chamber does not oppose the modifications to the list of witnesses contained in those requests. However, once again some concerns arise from these changes. In particular, the Chamber is concerned about the estimate for the evidence of the last two witnesses mentioned in the fourth request, that is the protected witness named in the confidential annex to the Defence request of the 2nd of March, 2006, and Milovan Bjelica. In the view of the Chamber, the time foreseen for their testimony will not allow the Defence to finish their evidence by the 4th of April, 2006, the date set by the Scheduling Order. Depending on the exact date of Milovan Bjelica's appearance in court, either a substantial amount of time us be gained in the examination of witnesses appearing before him, or a request to shorten the accused's testimony or its preparation must be for the coming. The Chamber therefore asks the Defence to take these remarks into consideration, and this concludes the Chambers's response to the third and fourth requests for guidance.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no comment on that at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Maricic, please be seated. Mr. Maricic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Harmon, the counsel for the Prosecution. And where I think I'd forgotten this morning to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony, I take it that you understood that you're still bound by it. I see you are nodding yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That doesn't appear on the transcript, but it's now confirmed. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Maricic.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Maricic -- first of all, if we could pass out the bundles of exhibits. Mr. Maricic, you're going to receive in front of you a bundle of exhibits that have tab numbers, and I'm going to direct you to certain documents behind each of the tabs, and then I'm going to ask you to consult those documents. I'll direct you to certain portions of it, of the documents I'd like you to read, and if there is no translation then I will read the English version of the documents to you and then ask for your comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, your microphone is still open, and I --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And if the witness could be presented the first bundle.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Maricic, you testified that you were on the Main Board of the SDS in Brcko in the first year -- sorry, the Main Board of the SDS --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, if I may interrupt you. It seems as if a similar noise comes with your microphone. I don't know. Perhaps it's equality of arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Is this any better, Your Honour? This is a different microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's better.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'll use this microphone then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it's good if the Prosecutor's computer makes a similar noise as the Defence computer. It's not completely over, but I think it's better, at least. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Maricic, you testified that you were on the Main Board of the SDS in its first year of existence, 1990 to 1991. Let me turn your attention to tab 1, the document in tab 1. This document is P529, tab 455, for the record. Mr. Maricic, this is a list of the members of the Main Board of the Serbian Democratic Party in Bosnia. You'll notice that your name is at item number 21, and handwritten next to your name is the name of Dr. Vojinovic Marinko. Did you and Dr. Vojinovic Marinko share responsibilities at the Main Board of the SDS in 1990 and 1991?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it was called the Main Board. Second, when I was member of the Main Board, Dr. Milenko Vojinovic was not a member of the Main Board at the same time. We could not have shared responsibilities because he was not a member then. Replaced me on the Main Board. And when he was appointed, I stopped being a member of the Main Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How many Main Board meetings did you attend in 1990 and 1991?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you that, but I attended a rather large number of meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Now, in your evidence yesterday - this is found Your Honours, at page 45 of LiveNote, lines 5 and 6 - you said that you were surprised to find out that he, being Mr. Krajisnik, was a member of the Main Board since it was founded. If you look at this list, this document in tab 1, you don't see Mr. Krajisnik's name at all. So my question to you is: What is the source of your information that Mr. Krajisnik was a member of the Main Board since it was founded?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had some sort of paper from some sort of Prosecution, and that's where I read that Mr. Krajisnik had been a member of the Main Board since its foundation. And I can only say again that I was surprised if he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you see -- in the years 1990 and 1991, did you see Mr. Krajisnik attending the meetings of the Main Board of the SDS that you attended?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1990 and 1991, I never saw Mr. Krajisnik anywhere, including the sessions of the Main Board. Which doesn't mean he wasn't there, but I didn't see him speak, take the floor, or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: At the session of the SDS Main Board on the 21st of July, 1991, there was an election and -- of Main Board members. Your name -- you were not elected in that session. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that session. I know that I received notification. I probably didn't attend, but I was notified that Dr. Beli came to replace me with the explanation that as president of the Municipal Board he should occupy that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honours, found in tab 32 are excerpts from the SDS session of the Main Board. It's P37, and it identifies the people who were elected to the Main Board at that session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Maricic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, if I look to tab 32, the description does not fit, Mr. Harmon, for purposes of -- I don't know whether this was how it was originally filed. I would have to check that. Because it gives comment rather than just what the document is. The document is the transcript of the SDS session of the 21st of July, and its comment that Mr. Maricic was not elected, just as it would be comment to say that I was not elected.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Then I'll withdraw the comment, Your Honour, and let the record speak for itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Maricic, after you were replaced on the Main Board by Dr. Beli, did you ever attend another SDS Main Board meeting?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention now, sir, to the document that's found in tab 31 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Maricic would like to say something, Mr. Harmon, please. Mr. Maricic, please. He raised his hand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By a strange coincidence, when Dr. Beli died I became deputy to the Assembly of the Republika Srpska in his stead and member of the Main Board, again in his stead, and I think it was in 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You'd say you then again attended other SDS Main Board meetings, whereas I take it, Mr. Harmon, you were interested to know about the early years rather than --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I was interested in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that was not part of your question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness, if you could kindly turn to the document that is found in tab 31. This is a document that is not in your language, so I will read this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it needs a number first.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 31, Your Honours, P1118.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I would not be surprised since you were not always happy with press articles, but I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness, I will identify this document. This is a document that is from the time you --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- service?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, the approach I have personally taken as Your Honour has seen over the last few weeks is that I allow other than exceptional circumstances the questions to be put and then make my submissions in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is a document, Mr. Maricic, that is from the Tanjug news service. It's from August 28, 1997 entitled settlement in Brcko settling. I'll read some paragraphs. It says, the first paragraph: "The situation in the Bosnian Serb town of Brcko was slowly settling in the early evening of Thursday and the people were dispersing from the streets. However, two more civilians were hurt in shooting by SFOR in the afternoon. Local municipal authorities have held brief meetings with officials some international institutions. SFOR troop movements have slowed down but reconnaissance flights are continuous. And I'm going to read the penultimate paragraph. "During the afternoon the municipal Brcko council held an emergency session to discussion the situation and decided to issue a statement inviting the people to exercise restraint and return to their homes. In view of the fact that Brcko public safety centre chief Andrija Bjelosevic has disappeared from town the Municipal Council has in a summary procedural appointed Bosko Maricic the first commander of the Serb Territorial Defence of Brcko to be acting chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It doesn't say "the," and the absence of the "the" might be significant on this occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I said "the," then I withdraw that and I'm reading --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps these --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I was going to say, it's going to make interpreting extremely difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- re-read the sentence then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you read it very slowly and now the interpreters are alerted on possible problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. View of the fact that Brcko public safety centre chief Andrija Bjelosevic has disappeared from town the Municipal Council has in a summary procedure appointed Bosko Maricic 1st commander of the Serb Territorial Defence of Brcko to be acting chief." Mr. Maricic, were you the 1st commander of the Serb Territorial Defence of Brcko?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have an official appointment, and I don't know anything about it, and I don't know which year you are talking about, but there was no official appointment. I don't remember that, nor did I command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were you ever unofficially given the tasks of directing, commanding the Territorial Defence in the Serb Territorial Defence in the Brcko municipality?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think the witness is entitled to the year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Harmon, if you look at the year at the top of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm asking him a very general question, if he was ever a Serb -- acted in the capacity of commander --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's fair for the witness to be aware. Your earlier questions were about 1990, 1991, whereas the focus of his testimony has been completely on say years before 1995, then it's fair that the witness who has not the text of this report in front of him in a language which is his own to confront him explicitly with the year expressed on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'll do it by a number of years, then, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In 1998 were you ever the commander of the Serb Territorial Defence in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In 1991, were you ever given a position either de facto or de jure as the commander of the Serb Territorial Defence in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing of any appointment, and I know for sure that I never commanded. I told you all about the various things I did during the war, and I was on the front line from the first day of the war as a simple soldier. I don't know if it was ever discussed, but I never received any official document appointing me, nor did I act as a commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But now to get it quite clear, Mr. Maricic, were you ever informed, whether you received a document or not, whether it was by the neighbours, whether it was by the chief of staff, were you ever informed about you being appointed in a commanding position in the TO whether prior to the war, during the war, or after the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me turn to a different part of your evidence. You testified yesterday that you were the SDS vice-president. Can you tell me the dates when you functioned as the vice-president of the SDS in your municipality?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but think it was the end of July or the beginning of August in 1990 when the founding Assembly of the SDS was held in Brcko, and at that meeting, the SDS was founded, either at that Assembly or a few days later when the leadership was elected. Dr. Beli received the largest number of votes for the position of president, and I received the largest number of votes for vice-president. I think it was held in a hall. It wasn't at the founding Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Maricic, you're describing how you were appointed. The question was the dates when you functioned. When did it approximately start? I do understand it was the end of July or beginning of August 1990. Until when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, my official function ceased when I was sent for treatment. I couldn't discharge any functions while I was being treated, and later I was severely disabled. So you could say that it ended in May 1992. So you could say that I was vice-president from 1990 to May 1992, although I'm not sure I understood the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you did not take up that office again once you returned to Brcko in September 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, by that time the SDS did not really operate any more, and I was severely disabled. I was wondering how I would earn my livelihood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the question was whether you were still or again in that function once you returned. Whether it was very active is another matter, but formally were you in that position once you returned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I was, because I don't remember being replaced or dismissed from that position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed. And could you, Mr. Maricic, listen carefully to what you are asked, then focus your answer specifically on the question. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let's turn to a different exhibit. Witness, if you'd turn to the Exhibit that is found in tab 24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which needs a number as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 24 will be P1119.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness, this is a page from the Official Gazette, and I'm going to direct your attention the right-hand column, the number 298. Witness, this exhibit indicates that pursuant to Article 80 of the Republika Srpska Constitution of the decision on the creation of War Presidencies in municipalities during a state of war, then it gives a number, the president of the republic passed the following decision on the creation of a war Presidency in Brcko municipality. And if we look at item number 6, it indicates that Bosko Maricic was a member, and this was dated the 30th of July, 1995, and the typed signature -- the typed name of Dr. Radovan Karadzic, president of the republic, appears under it. Were you in fact appointed to the War Presidency, the Brcko War Presidency, on this date and did you function this that capacity?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm seeing this for the first time. I'm sure that I didn't attend a single session. It was very late in 1995, and I don't know anything about this, although I see my name here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Let's turn to a different document then, Witness. Can you tell me what is the municipal association of participants in the war in 1990?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must be some mistake. I don't know what kind of association of participants in the war could have existed in 1990. Maybe communist participants.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... tab 22, Witness. This also needs a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 22 would be P1120.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness, this document, tab 22, is a document from the East Bosnia Corps. It's strictly confidential. It was addressed to Major General Gvero. It was on the subject of information relating to certain events in Brcko, and it is signed by the commander, Major General Novica Simic. And I want to direct your -- let me just refresh your recollection perhaps as to what this document is about. This document, Witness, dealt with certain claims made by Mr. Djordje Ristanic who was president of the Brcko Municipal Assembly that he addressed to the East Bosnia Corps on the 5th of October, 1993, and he particularly stressed that there was a danger that the president of the municipality of Brcko may be removed by certain municipal boardsmen who are within the 1st Posavina Brigade. As a result of that, on the 6th of October, there were a series of conversations with various people who were identified in this document, including yourself, and this -- the interviews were conducted by a commission. If we return, Witness, to the account of the interview made with you, and if you take a look at the B/C/S version in front you, Mr. Maricic, it is on the second page of the text, the second large paragraph starting with "U nazgo voru sa Boskom Maricicem." That's the text I want to direct your attention to, and I want to direct Your Honour's attention to page 3 of the English version, the first paragraph, the first full paragraph starting with "During our conversation with Bosko Maricic, vice-president of the SDS and president of the association of participants in the war in 1990," and then that's -- can you enlighten us as to what that particular association is, Mr. Maricic?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a mistake. This association was established in 1992, I believe, and it is true that I was elected its president.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. So this is a typographical error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was the name of the association participants in the war in 1992? Was that then the name of the ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this should be the case, because in 1990 and 1991, there were no war veterans and there could not be a name of that sort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness, then let me ask you then to turn to tab 47, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which needs a number as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 47 will be P1121.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I would like to direct your attention to the article with the headline from Brcko to Ravna Gora. And this appears in a publication, Brcanski pogledi, dated the 28th of April, 1994, and I will read part of this document. 53 years ago, on 12 April 1941 to be precise, Draza Mihajlovic spent some time in our town. On that occasion the Serb Chetnik Association of Brcko commemorated this date with a small celebration. On behalf of the Serbian Chetnik organisation, Mr. Bosko Maricic addressed those gathered at the old railway station, the place where the legendary Chetnik general had addressed the people and Serbian heroes," and then it goes on to quote you. Were you -- you represent the Serbian Chetnik organisation? Were you a member of the Serbian Chetnik organisation, Mr. Maricic?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a member. I was a member. And that was for a while, and later on I discontinued my membership.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When did you become a member of the Serbian Chetnik organisation?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbian Chetnik organisation was established in Brcko and it had nothing whatsoever to do with any parties. I don't know when its founding session took place, but I can assume that it was towards the end of 1992 or in 1993. I don't know. Maybe you have the exact date somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Why did you join the Serbian Chetnik organisation?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Draza Mihajlovic was the leader of democratic forces in the Second World War, and my father was a member of those forces. So it was only logical for me to continue that affiliation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, you testified in response to a question yesterday by Mr. Josse that you were a member of the Bosnian Serb Assembly in 1994. And I saw on your testimony earlier this morning, during my examination you said 1995, and I want to clarify that evidence so the record is perfectly clear, Mr. Maricic. You replaced Dr. Beli in the Bosnian Serb Assembly after he died. That's the case, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if we -- I would like to show you, Witness, just to orient you as to time and to be perfectly clear, if we turn to tab 25, Witness, this is P65 tab 128, also P529, tab 49. This is a transcript of a tape recording, Witness, from the 50th session of the national assembly that was held on the 15th and 16th of April 1995 in Sanski Most. And if you look at the B/C/S version, sir, on the -- what appears to have the number 10 at the top of the page and bears the ERN 00845892, you'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm referring to the -- page bottom at the bottom says 132 of 389.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You will see that Dr. Vojinovic appears to be alive and well on that date because he's addressing the Assembly. Do you have any reason to dispute the date which Dr. Beli addressed the Assembly that's recorded in this document?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is true. He was still an Assembly member at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Then if we could turn then to -- Witness, if we could turn to the document that is found in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, if you would just have asked the witness whether 1994 was a mistake and it was actually 1995. It would have saved us a couple of pages copied and et cetera, et cetera. Of course, you could have them in reserve in case --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'll be glad to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were you appointed in 1995, Witness, to the Bosnian Serb Assembly?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Beli felt poorly at this meeting in Sanski Most because of some clash with generals. He went to hospital then. Maybe a month, two months later he died, and some time later I became an Assembly member. And this is the truth and I can't be sure of the exact time when all this happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, let me show you then Witness let me show you an exhibit in tab 27.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It needs an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 27 would be P1122.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If you could turn to that, Mr. Maricic. I direct your attention to the left-hand column the item of the gazette that is numbered 276.
