This is a decision verifying the mandates of deputies in the National Assembly, and it is a decision that was passed on the 6th of August, 1995, and is signed by the President of the National Assembly, Momcilo Krajisnik. Does this refresh your recollection as to the date when you were appointed to the national Bosnian Serb Assembly?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't remember the date, but this decision may have passed even after the Assembly meeting. I attended the Assembly meeting when I was appointed an Assembly member. I -- I can't remember the date. But this -- this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me then -- when you say this is correct, are you saying that this is the date -- this is the correct date when you were appointed to the Bosnian Serb Assembly?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not talking about the date. I'm talking about the body of the text containing my name. This decision may have been passed even after the relevant Assembly session. What I'm saying is this is when it was officially drawn up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Just in case, Your Honour, I'm turning to tab 26 so we can eliminate any doubt. If we turn to tab 26, Witness, this needs a new number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1123.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's still not clear to me, Mr. Harmon. I mean, we're now moving from 1994 to 1995. I don't know. I take it that something important would have happened during those years and it's not just a matter of not knowing exactly when he started.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, it is a matter of clarification, Your Honour, and precision because this witness has opined about certain matters in connection with his contacts with Mr. Krajisnik. He's put the date of 1994. It's our submission that Mr. Maricic was appointed on the 6th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We will make that submission based on two documents, the document P1123 which is the text of the Assembly session. It was held on the 6th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand what you're doing, the relevance and the importance, especially, of it is not yet clear to me but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I understand. I'm trying not to dwell too much on the issue and I'm trying to get through it as quickly as possible. The witness has said that he doesn't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So if we could take a look, witness, at the document in tab 26. This is the minutes of the 52nd session of the national assembly of Republika Srpska held on the 6th of August, 1995. And, Witness, when -- what I'd like to do is direct your attention to the session -- if we turn, if you turn, Witness, to the second page of the Cyrillic text, the large paragraph -- large paragraph that appears slightly below the mid-line, it says --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I'm referring to page 3 of the English page 3 of 149.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The text reads, "in the meantime we were also discussing the appointment of a deputy who should replace the deceased Vojinovic. There is a preliminary agreement this should also be a candidate from the list, a person who passed the elections, and who is also from Brcko. Can we do the last selection and appointment without verification or we should get the opinion of the Main Board for this candidate. Mr. Maricic is here." And it goes on. Mr. Maricic, does that reflect your recollection of the session where you were appointed to replace Mr. Vojinovic as a member of the Bosnian Serb Assembly?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was then, and I now remember that there was a discussion to that effect when my appointment was being discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So you accept, do you, then, Mr. Maricic, that your appointment -- you were replacing Mr. Vojinovic as of the 6th of August, 1995. That's not in dispute, is it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise for having misspoken, for having mentioned 1994. It was a long time ago. I can't remember the date. I am even wrong when it comes to some years, apparently.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Maricic, you testified that the war -- you became the director of a local furniture factory. Was that the Majevica factory in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could turn to tab 42. This needs a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 42, Your Honours, will be P1124.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This document is not in your language so I will read it -- portions of it to you and then ask you to affirm whether it's correct or not. This is a press release from the Office of the High Representative dated the 25th of July, 2002, and it reads: "OHR press release. Supervisor of Brcko request replacement of director and steering board of Majevica. Supervisor of Brcko, Henri L. Clarke, has asked Brcko district mayor Sinisa Kisic to replace Mr. Bosko Maricic, director of ODP Majevica Brcko and its steering board, following the action of the Prosecutor's office in seeking the confirmation of an indictment against Mr. Maricic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: "The indictment charges Mr. Maricic with abuse of office and failure to carry out his official duties by permitting the illegal construction of residences on Majevica property for himself and another 30 families between January 2000 and May 2002 without payment of any compensation for the land or obtaining construction licenses." That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I withdraw question. I can see Mr. Josse standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My objection is that, in my submission, the whole of this document needs to be read to the witness. If he's going to be cross-examined on this issue, bearing in mind it's not in his language, he's entitled to have it all read to him. That's what I submit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I -- Mr. Harmon, I don't know how this is put in the sequence of your questions, but I would suggest that it's fair to the witness that it will be read and translated to him, but at the same time to spend all this time -- all that time on it in court -- Mr. Josse, would it be a fair solution if we would ask one of our interpreters in the next break to read and translate this document to the witness and he can ask parts to be repeated, et cetera. And then, Mr. Harmon, I don't know to what extent it would interrupt the -- interrupt your sequence of questions, but at the same time I would say this is not a document where you were dependent on the 65 ter summary, I take it, knowing the name and the position of the accused. I mean, this could have been sent for translation --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This could have been sent for translation at an earlier stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We just received this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You just received it. Yes. In that case -- nevertheless, I suggest that it will be read to the witness during the next break so that he's fully aware of the content of the whole of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If an interpreter is good enough to do that we would be very grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll see whether someone would be available. Mr. Harmon. But, of course -- apart from asking the witness to read, of course you could put questions to the witness in relation to this matter even without confronting him with the document and nevertheless he would be given an opportunity to further comment once he has received an oral translation of the document. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct, isn't it, Mr. Maricic? The supervisor of Brcko did request the mayor to replace you because you had been indicted, because he had sought confirmation of an indictment against you. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We turn to -- I don't have to turn to the document. And on that very same day you were dismissed. You were replaced on the order of the mayor. Mr. Kisic from the position of director of the Majevica factory. That's correct also isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Furthermore, Mr. Maricic, you were prosecuted for crimes in -- committed in the Republika Srpska in the municipality of Brcko in the lower court of Brcko district for the crime of abuse of official position. You were prosecuted and you were convicted of that crime. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was convicted. But whether I abused my position or not is rather debatable. I'm sure that I would have been given even a harsher sentence if the allegations were correct in the indictment. However, after a lengthy procedure, I was actually found almost not guilty. Actually, I got a very minimum fine of 4.500 German marks, which is peanuts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You were sentenced to three months imprisonment, isn't that correct, by the lower District Court?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was just fined. I'd had to pay 4.500 German marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we turn to tab 40. This document needs a new number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 40, Your Honours, will be P1125.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness, this is a document from the lower court of the Brcko -- BH Brcko district number KP 117/03 dated the 19th of March, 2004, and it is a judgement which you are found guilty for the crime of abuse of official position or authorisation from Article 337, paragraph 4, in relation to paragraph 3 of the Criminal Code of Republika Srpska. Witness, if you turn to -- I'm referring Your Honours to page 2 of the English version. Witness, this document reflects that you were sentenced to a term imprisonment of three months. It doesn't reflect a fine. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The verdict was a term of imprisonment of three months, but there is an additional sentence of the same lower court where the sentence is transformed into 4.500 German marks, but all that was overturned by a higher court in Brcko. Could you please find that sentence as well? I did not go to prison. I just paid 4.500 German marks. This sentence was altered by the higher court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we turn to tab 41. This needs a number as well?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1126.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness, this is the appeals court of the BH Brcko district and this is the judgement of the appeals court from the lower court decision?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, may I draw your attention to the fact at least in the sentence itself there are some mistakes which I see, numbers of a hundred becoming 100, three zeros, which suggests the comma replaced by a dot and a 0 added which gives a totally different impression on this -- on especially this sentence. Apart from whether it's a final one, but the translation is in this respect not very precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'll look into that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Look, Witness, at P1126, tab 41. This appears to be the appeals court judgement from the conviction from the lower court. And, Witness, we turn to the last paragraph in the B/C/S version, and I'm referring to page 6 of 6, it reads: "Since there are no reasons that disprove the first instant judgement either in the appeal of the BH public prosecutor's office of Brcko district or the Defence of Bosko Maricic, lawyer Milenko Simikic, pursuant to the provisions of Article 312 of the BH Brcko district Criminal Code, this court passed the decision as stated in which it rejected the aforementioned appeals as unfounded and confirmed the judgement reached at the first instance." So this appeals judgement, Witness, confirmed your conviction in the lower court. Do you dispute what's in this document, Mr. Maricic?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were there other legal proceedings after this appeals decision that you want to inform us about that may have resulted in a further modification of your sentence?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. The president of the court, a lady, passed a decision that the sentence prison would be altered into a fine of 4.500 German marks, but you are reading just the aggravating conditions. There are some other allegations of the second instance court stating that the Prosecutor's allegations were not correct, and you should read that. And also because of all this and also because of the fact that I was not guilty, and that is why the second instance court varied my sentence into a fine, which I paid. I didn't go to prison. Could you please look at the page number 3 where it says that the allegations made by the Prosecutor are not correct and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I've read this, Mr. Maricic. I've also read the conclusion of this document that affirms the conviction of you for the crimes. And while this document did reject some of the prosecutor's claims on appeal, it affirmed the conviction. I have no issue with what you have to say in terms of some of the prosecution's positions on appeal being rejected by the appeals court, but my question to you is: This judgement by the appeals court confirmed your conviction in the lower court, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to add something. The truth is also that the court made an official decision after the proceedings varying my prison sentence into a fine of 4.500 German marks. And this is also the truth. I didn't spend a single day in prison. And I'm really surprised that you haven't got that as well. I want --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Maricic, if you have a written document in your possession which -- in which a decision is contained which changes your term of imprisonment of -- to 4.500 convertible marks, German marks, then the Chamber would like to receive that. Yes? Have you got such a document in your possession at home or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Brcko this is part of my case file. This is an official document that was passed by the presiding judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have that decision in your possession at home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A practical way of getting it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will inquire -- we inquired and we were provided with these documents. I'll make a further inquiry, Your Honour. We received these documents from the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And if you would like to present this, perhaps once you've finished, Mr. Josse, if you would consider it relevant for this Court to know, then once you've finished your testimony here, so not before that, perhaps you can send a copy either through the victims and witness section or if you would find that easier through Mr. Josse, if at least, you would be available for that Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If the Defence team will liaise with Mr. Maricic, but I intend to re-examine on this issue anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And we will also make an inquiry, Your Honour, into the documents that we were provided and I'll make a further inquiry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, you had testified today about negotiations with the Muslims. Let me ask you, Mr. Maricic, to turn to tab 17 in this document, in this bundle of documents. And tab P529 Hanson tab 74. Mr. Maricic, this is a document, the summary of the events and situations within an assessment of the degree of achievement, and if you turn, Mr. Maricic, to the last page of this document in B/C/S, you'll see that it is signed by the War Presidency of the Brcko municipality?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, is this same document is P22 or -- I think it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, on page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. Apparently it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise that signature? Can you read the name?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is the signature of Djordje Ristanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. And what was his role in the War Presidency, Mr. Maricic?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that the War Presidency never actually operated. And I found somewhere where it says that the president of the War Presidency is Djordje Ristanic. There was not a single session of the War Presidency that formally existed that I attended, and I don't remember any. And I'm absolutely certain it never really operated apart from the president who was earlier president of the Assembly and maybe individual members did meet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, we'll come to the War Presidency in a few minutes, Mr. Maricic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But may I ask you, Mr. Maricic, is it now that you say Mr. Ristanic was a member of this War Presidency or was he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no evidence that he was elected president of the War Presidency, but some sort of logic tells me that since he used to be president of the Assembly and since I see his signature here that it was him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's only the basis of the information you have now that you come to this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very little was said about the War Presidency in Brcko, and I really don't know anything about it. It could have been established maybe at the beginning of the war when I was wounded, when I was absent from the area. I was severely disabled. Whether it held any sessions without me, I can't say, but I don't remember that I attended a single session of the War Presidency although it's a possibility. But many years have passed since then. And there was general chaos in Brcko at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you know that it exist.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you not sure whether you know it, or do you say I -- it's not sure that it did exist.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not sure whether I know, and I can't say with any certainty whether it existed or not. I am more inclined to say that it did. But since I'm not absolutely sure, I don't want to speculate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Maricic, according to your earlier testimony genocide was committed against the Serbs in Brcko municipality in the Second World War. As a result of that, the Serbs in Brcko considered the territory of Brcko to be Serbian because it was a place where genocide had been committed against the Serbs. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think you could put it that way. The Serbs did not think that Brcko should belong to the Serbs, nor was anything done in the course of this latest war because of something that happened in World War II.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, let's take a look at this document that's in front of you in tab 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, where exactly did the witness say that -- I don't remember the word genocide, but maybe that I'm wrong. A search in yesterday and today's transcript does not assist me. I saw similar words in the 65 ter summary. I don't know whether you are --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me just -- bear with me for one minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have some notes, and I'll see if I can locate the reference. I'm recalling the witness testified yesterday about Serbs being killed by Muslims during the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, which of course is not the same yet as ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me see if I can find the reference, Your Honour. It certainly appears in the 65 ter summary, Your Honour. It certainly appears in the 65 ter summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but if -- we'd rather not use the 65 ter summary because that would raise a few questions as well, such as numbers of those killed in September and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm not able to find it, Your Honour, in my notes, and certainly I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My search -- and usually if I search on the 22nd, then I get it in your question, but I do not find it in 21st.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, then I'll rephrase the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Maricic, did you ever hear articulated the position that territory where genocide was committed against the Serbs in the Second World War, the territory where that genocide had taken place was Serb territory, historically Serb territory? Did you ever hear of that position ever being taken or articulated by anybody in the SDS or anybody in a leadership position?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I didn't hear it only from the SDS. It was a generally taken position that, looking back, Brcko was originally Serb, a Serb town, and it was later on that Muslims moved in, migrated into Brcko and started pushing Serbs out. That is not speculation. That's a historical fact. I read history of Brcko, and it is written clearly how Islamists or, rather, Muslims moved into Brcko. Before that time, there were no other people in Brcko but Christians.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was it your view, Witness, that genocide did take place against the Serbs and the Jews in the Brcko municipality during the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to avoid the term "genocide" because it's a very controversial term that has to do with numbers. I recently listened to an international scientist who opposes the term being used even in relation to Srebrenica. However, I would say that a massacre did take place during the Second World War. It was done. It is no secret, and it is easily verifiable. I mentioned the bridge across the Sava River where mass liquidations took place. First of all, Jews were almost completely liquidated and then Serbs as well. It was said at the time during World War II that one-third of the Serbs would be killed, one-third would be converted to Catholicism, and one third would be expelled. And there are many mass graves and former execution sites where you can see monuments -- monuments stand to go this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness, I want to direct your attention back to the document we've been looking at document in tab 17 the document signed by Mr. Ristanic. Witness, I want to read a portion of this text to you. Witness, it says as follows -- I'm referring, Your Honours, to the text at the top of page 2 in the English. Witness, I'm afraid I cannot orient you in your -- on the document in front of you. Let me see if I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you have the exact portion, Mr. Harmon, then we'll be able to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which in the English would you --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It's the second -- essentially, the bullet point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The ethnic balance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The ethnic balance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. I'll assist you in finding it. It's on page 2, the second paragraph from the -- no. Let me just see. Yes. You'll find the bullet points on the lower part of page 2 in the B/C/S. And you'll find the number 16 there clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I see it, Your Honour. My document is incomplete in my package but I have another one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Mr. Harmon is directing your attention to page 2 of this document, the third bullet point from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And it reads, Witness: "The ethnic balance of the population of Brcko is unfavourable (especially since the arrival of 16.000 people from Sandzak). It is artificially created over a longer period, organised so that Serbian villages are spread out in a different Posavina -- in different Posavina municipalities with the goal of making the Serbs a minority everywhere despite the fact that they have always occupied and owned the largest part of the territory." So I return to my question to you, Mr. Maricic. The Serbs prior to the outbreak of the war believed that the territory of Brcko was Serb territory in large measure, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only historically speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, furthermore, Mr. Maricic, the Serbs certainly considered that the territory of Brcko was strategically important?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Serbs believed it, and so did Muslims and Croats, and that's the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now -- well, let me read to you then the paragraph that's directly above the paragraph that I just -- or two paragraphs above the paragraph I just referred you to. It's -- the paragraph I'm referring to Your Honour is the bottom of page 1 in the English. "It should be mentioned that the leadership was aware throughout the period of the strategic importance of Brcko municipality which was conveyed to the population and presented to the leadership of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." And then it goes on. Now, Witness, there were discussions, weren't there, before the start of the war with the leadership of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina about the importance of Brcko. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that's correct. Reading this text, I understand that the man who wrote this is terribly afraid that something awful might happen to Serbs in Brcko. I don't see that he's writing anything about strategic importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me read the paragraph to you again, then, Witness. "It should be mentioned that the leadership was aware throughout the period of the strategic importance of the Brcko municipality which was conveyed to the population and presented to the leadership of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." This document, prepared by Mr. Ristanic, says that the leadership was aware of Brcko's strategic importance and that its strategic importance was presented to them. That's the case, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What it says here is that the leadership in Brcko, meaning the leadership of the Serbs in Brcko, was aware of it and drew the attention of the superior authorities to the fact. That's how I understand this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: My next question, Mr. Maricic, is to whom of the superior authorities did they draw the strategic importance of Brcko?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when he's asking for assistance, maybe he's exaggerating a bit, but we can see from this that it was brought to the attention of Republika Srpska leadership. And I have nothing to add to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Who was that, Witness? Who comprised the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, let's -- let's keep it as factual as possible. Do you know when and how it was brought to the attention of the Republika Srpska leadership?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I never even saw this paper until today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, analysing documents of which a witness says he doesn't know anything about it, the document is in evidence, and the Chamber of course is perfectly able to read it, to interpret it, and if someone who would have any specific knowledge about it could assist us, fine. If not, let's not engage in textual analysis of these kind of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- at this -- at this moment. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now I want to turn to a slightly different topic, Mr. Maricic. Before the war did you participate in discussions with the Muslims and the Croats from Brcko about dividing the municipality?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I know that some talks did take place, but I don't remember taking part in any of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Who took part in those discussions on behalf of the Bosnian Serbs from Brcko?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main man of the Bosnian Serbs in Brcko was Dr. Beli. No doubt about it. So it must have been him, and he must have solicited the assistance of some other lower-ranking people but not me. At least not that I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Are you aware --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, again. Mr. Maricic, you say, "So it must have been him." Do you know that he was involved in these negotiations or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that even he took part in the talks. I know -- I heard that talks were held. I can't say anything for sure about anyone. All I know is that talks were held.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And when you heard that, did you also hear that Dr. Beli was involved in these talks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. But I heard that talks were held, and I even heard that a line was drawn across the town for purposes of division.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who told you this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. It was a long time ago. It was a rumour that talks were going on about dividing the town. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, of course I do not know what the sequence of your questions would be, but let's not find out what rumours went around town.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm just exploring whether he participated in them, and now I've been informed that they're rumours. So I don't intend to go further than that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I want to focus, Witness, on one final subject, and that was the rhetoric that has been -- we've heard about in this courtroom about Serb leaders and Serbs in various municipalities saying that, "We can no longer live together with the Muslims. We can't live with the Croats." Was there similar types of rhetoric in the Brcko municipality, a rhetoric that was one that wanted to separate from -- the Serbs to separate from the Muslims and the Croats?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It existed then and it exists still, and it may be even stronger today.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you ever hear Dr. Beli express such -- such views?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you ever express such views?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a long time ago. I still believe that there is very little likelihood of creating a single state there without any separate entities, and I'm not going to dispute that I may have said something to that effect, because I still think it's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, can you -- I'm not sure what time you're going to take a recess but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Soon, but if you find the right moment within the next couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, this is the right moment then, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then -- yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness could take his headphones off for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It does seem that the witness understands some English. That's at least what I could --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think very little and it's not going to matter a great deal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we need the witness for after the -- if you -- yes. While the witness has his earphones on, yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's position as far as tab 42 is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I like to submit now that tab should not be submitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The witness has accepted that he was convicted of this matter. The documents that relate to his conviction I don't object to, both the first instance and the appellate court. And as I've already said I intend to ask him some more questions about it. But Mr. Harmon put a proposition to he didn't need the document to put that proposition to the witness. The witness readily accepted that he was involved or he was convicted of that particular allegation. Thereafter, tab 42 really is a different aspect of the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I would invite the Chamber to make a decision about this now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's ask first Mr. Harmon. Mr. Harmon, the document, as far as I can see, and I'm drawing your attention to the fourth full paragraph, "the supervisor's request is no indication of Mr. Maricic's guilt or innocence." It says because the charges are there we know what happened with the charges, that at that stage of the proceedings, I do understand that they considered it an appropriate administrative measure to be taken. I mean, I don't know what that adds to what we now know about the proceedings and also what we now know since the witness has told us. So is there any need at this moment for the witness to read the whole of the document and I'm certain will draw our attention very much to this paragraph and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, there isn't any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then do I then understand that there's no need to tender this document any more, that there's no need for the witness to read it? Of course, if the witness would like to read it, fine, but I take it the matter has been dealt with sufficiently.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If the document don't go into evidence I don't need to re-examine him upon it and I'm content with that. I don't think an interpreter need trouble him or herself reading it to Mr. Maricic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The parties agree on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it will not be tendered. There is no question about the admission. Mr. Maricic. You don't have to read the document. The document will not be used by the Court. It will not be presented. The document you were invited to read during the break, we'll just discard that. But we'll have a break. We'll have a break until ten minutes to one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, please proceed. Yes, I said please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't hear you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Maricic, I want to direct your attention to the document at tab 17 again. It's P529, Hanson tab 74. I want to direct your attention to page 2 in the Cyrillic text.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I would like to direct Your Honours' attention to page 1 of the penultimate paragraph on page 1 of the English testing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness, in the middle of the paragraph, the portion that starts with "In this context the Assembly of the Serbian municipality of Brcko..." Do you see that in the middle of the page? It has a date of April 29, 1992. I'll read the text to you, Witness. It says: "In this context it, the Assembly of the Serbian municipality of Brcko was convened on 29 April 1992 at which an analysis and an assessment of the achieved situation were given and of the War Presidency was elected to which all powers of the Assembly were transferred until peacetime conditions are created." So according to this document that was prepared by Mr. Ristanic, the War Presidency was created the day before the war started in Bosnia -- in Brcko, I'm sorry. Why was -- why was the War Presidency created the day before the war started in Brcko, Mr. Maricic?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not attend that session, and I cannot tell you anything about it. I can't even say why it was established. At least I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was it -- forget that. Now, you said in your evidence, Witness, that the war started with the blowing up of the bridges in Brcko, and you further testified that you had no clue that the bridges were going to be blown up.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In the intervening 14 years since those bridges were blown up, have you heard or received any information as to who blew up those bridges, Mr. Maricic?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The war did not start with the blowing up of the bridges but the day after. And as far as the explosions of the bridges, it was some sort of taboo. I personally never tried to find out anything about it. I wasn't interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It was the position of the SDS, wasn't it, Mr. Maricic, that the bridges should be blown up in order to protect the people in Brcko by incursion by the Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In fact, I put to you, Mr. Maricic, that members of the SDS leadership in Brcko went to the JNA commander and asked them -- asked him to blow up those bridges for precisely that reason, for security of the Serb population in Brcko. That's the case, isn't it, Witness?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not disputing that, but I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, before the bridges were blown up, Mr. Maricic, you said that you went and visited a village by the name of Stanovi. You visited a friend the night before the explosion. Who is the friend you visited?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gasa Chetnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Gasa Chetnik, is that the name?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you tell us, where was it you stayed in the village of Stanovi?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This Gasa Chetnik, it is probably not his real name. That's how we called him. He was elderly man, and he was a Chetnik during the Second World War, and I stayed in Gasa's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you stay with anybody else from the municipality of Brcko?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on that day. I don't remember. I wouldn't say anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, it's a fact, isn't it, Mr. Maricic, that you and Mr. Djordje Ristanic and a gentleman by the name of Dragan Veselic were relocated to the village of Stanovi just before the bridges were blown up? You were relocated there by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was informed by somebody that I should seek shelter. I went there. I saw Djordje Ristanic there but not Dragan Veselic. And I saw Djordje because I was walking by. There was a school building. He was there. I don't remember Dragan Veselic being there, and I wouldn't say that he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Who told you to relocate to the village of Stanovi?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who told me that, and I was never clear why I was said that. I didn't want to seek shelter, but somebody told me to do that and I did it. I suppose that it was somebody wearing a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It was somebody from the JNA, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I can't confirm this. Somebody told me. He may even have worn civilian clothes. Somebody told me; I obeyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. So who else besides you were told to go to Stanovi the day before the bridges were blown up?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anybody else. I saw Djordje Ristanic there. Somebody must have told him as well. And I don't remember anybody else that I saw there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It's a fact, isn't it, Mr. Maricic, that you were told that the bridges were going to be blown up before they were actually blown up? You were told by the garrison commander of the JNA that the bridges were to be blown up and that you and Mr. Ristanic and Mr. Veselic should relocate to an area outside of Brcko. That's the fact, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I was never told this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, did you ever make any inquiry, Mr. Maricic, as to why you were to be relocated six kilometres outside of Brcko? You seem to be a man of strong views and a quite man of independent views. Why was it, Mr. Maricic, that you acquiesced to go with somebody to a village, Stanovi, immediately before the bridges were blown up?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never been able to get to the bottom of this. I suppose I bothered somebody and it was some sort of a game that somebody played.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And how soon after the bridges were blown up, Mr. Maricic, was it that you returned to the village of Brcko -- to the town of Brcko?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All this happened 15 years ago. On the following day, I got into a car and returned to Brcko immediately after the explosions to see what had happened. I took my own car to go to Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's proceed to a different topic, then, Mr. Maricic. Let's take about paramilitary formations, because your evidence yesterday -- I'm referring the Court to page 54, lines 15 through 24. You were asked by Mr. Josse about paramilitary formations, about the arrival of them, and your evidence was you knew very little about their arrival. Such things were kept secret from you, and you only saw them in small numbers in town. And then you were asked by Mr. Josse about certain paramilitary formations. You were asked about Captain Dragan, you were asked about Arkan's forces, and you were asked about Mauzer. Those questions, Your Honour, are pages 61 to 63. You were not asked by Mr. Josse nor did you comment about the paramilitary forces under the command of Mirko Blagojevic. You know Mr. Blagojevic, don't you, Mr. Maricic?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: His forces were also present in Brcko, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard they were there, but I never saw them. Maybe they were there while I was on the front line. However, on one occasion I did come across Mirko Blagojevic in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And you know Mr. Blagojevic, don't you?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you have any reason to dispute him as -- strike that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let's play a video if we can, please. This is -- will be found, Your Honour, tab 43, and it is Exhibit 727, tab 3. I'm sorry, it's tab 4 in the bundle, Your Honour. And I'm going to be referring -- before you start playing this, if I can direct Your Honours' attention to the portion that I'm going to be playing. In the evening learning version, Your Honour, it's on page 13, and it starts at the counter number 02:37:51, and goes over to -- actually, it starts at 02:37:33. It starts at that location. And Witness for your benefit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 9 out of 18, I take it. No, no, it's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In the B/C/S, Your Honour, it is on page 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 12, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness -- I'll wait until this text gets in front of you, Witness. Page 12, the counter number is 02:37:51. We'll play this now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no sound, Your Honour. I don't know if Your Honours are getting sound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have nothing at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let's start again. I've been given a signal that it's all right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover]. "Interviewer: My guest -- his truth. Our guest is Mirko Blagojevic. We talked a little about this war in Bijeljina but we managed to shed some light on all that. However, he did not fight only in Bijeljina. He responded to the call of the Serbian people also in other places in Republika Srpska where things were rough. Where was it the most difficult? "Blagojevic: Well, the main battle that we won from Semberija, have won addition to the battle for Bijeljina was the battle for Brcko. For us, winning the battle for Brcko was important, because seasoned Ustasha fighters had already been dispatched to Brcko from Croatia and Gunja and the bridge. And had they succeeded in taking Brcko, it would have been very difficult for people in Krajina and for us to join up. So we got there like lightning. Serbs, Croats and Muslims lived in Brcko. The Serbs were poorly organised there, in the town, and they were very much exposed to the danger of genocide. Fortunately, we arrived at the war theatre at the right moment. We put ourselves at the disposal of the then Crisis Staff of the Municipal Assembly of Brcko, of Serbian Brcko, of Mr. Bosko Maricic. And we said we were at their disposal and that he should tell us what needed to be done and where, but that we had to act like lightning. History wouldn't wait. What was done was done. The wheel of history could not be turned back. We had good cooperation with the then officers who were at the barracks in Brcko."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Maricic, do you recognise Mr. Blagojevic, the paramilitary leader?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: For Your Honours' reference, I refer Your Honours to the Prosecution Exhibit 1090 that we listened to in testimony of Mr. Poplasen. It identifies also Mr. Blagojevic who was one of the new Chetnik commanders who was honoured. I believe that for Your Honours' reference who this man was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, in fact, Mr. Maricic, Mr. Blagojevic put his forces at your disposal, didn't he, and the disposal of the war -- the Crisis Staff, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Blagojevic made all this up. I cannot believe that he stated this. I heard of his statement, but I never asked him about it. None of this is true. The truth is that I didn't see Blagojevic when he arrived in Brcko. I saw him once during the war in town, only him, nobody else. I don't know when he came, with how many people. I only heard that they had some problems surrounding theft, robbery. All this is a blatant lie. He could not find me because I was on the front line. How could he have locate -- located me?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let's talk about a different part of your testimony yesterday, Mr. Maricic. You were asked, Mr. Maricic, by Mr. Josse about the forces under the command of Captain Dragan, and your evidence, Mr. Maricic, found at page 62, lines 23 to 25, and 63, lines 1 to 2, you said: "I heard something at the beginning of the war and I even ran into three to four men," who you were told were under the command of Captain Dragan and you had no other information about his forces. Now, I want to refer you back, Mr. Maricic, to the document we've been looking at, at tab 17. It's Prosecution Exhibit 527 -- 529, Hanson tab 74. And I want to direct your attention -- refer -- refer Your Honours first of all, Your Honours, to page 3, two paragraphs up from the bottom and bear with me. I'm unable to direct you to the text, but I'm going to read the text to you, Mr. Maricic, in the document. Let me read it to you, Mr. Maricic. I'll read two paragraphs to you. "The largest part of the Serbian forces came from Semberija, Bijeljina, Ugljevik and they were mainly organised in two formations, the Serbian guard under the command of Ljubisa Savic, aka Mauzer and the radical under the command of Mirko Blagojevic. The first to arrive in Brcko was a group of instructors of Captain Dragan (Rade, Simo, Sasa, Bozo, Srdjo and others) and that was about four to six months before the war. They formed a special unit including a large number of Brcko residents who went through training. When the war started and during the combat activities, a number of members of this unit joined the Police Intervention Platoon, but the special unit grew to about 70 people." I won't read further. Mr. Maricic, you were aware of Captain Dragan and his men training Bosnian Serbs in the municipality of Brcko before the start of the war, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The leftists were in charge of all that organisation. This was under the control of the state security from Serbia. And I was not suitable for -- to learn about all this. So I only learnt about all that some 15 to 20 days before the war when two guys from Bukvik who told me they had been invited to join this training under Captain Dragan, and this is all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You weren't aware that they were there four to six months before the start of the war?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Where were they doing the training, Mr. Maricic?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only later, some years later, I heard that it was in the area of Razljevo, but I'm not sure even of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. These three to four young men who you encountered, were they the trainees of Dragan, Captain Dragan?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This must be a misunderstanding. I don't know what you're referring to. Which three or four young lads are you referring to in your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm referring --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The evidence is "two guys from Bukvik who told me that they had been invited to join this training." Were you referring to the two or to --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No. Let me just -- Your Honour, I'm referring to the evidence that was given by the witness yesterday. It's at page 62, line 23. "I even -- I heard sometime at the beginning of the war, and I even ran into three or four young men who I was told were under Captain Dragan." That's what I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Now it's -- yes. Yesterday, you testified, Mr. Maricic, "I even ran into three or four young men who I was told were under Captain Dragan, but I only ran into, like, three or four of them, not more." Now, the question by Mr. Harmon was whether these were trainees of Dragan, of Captain Dragan, were they trainees.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If that's how the question is worded, first of all let me tell you that the two guys from Bukvik did not join the training, and later on I learned that all of them had been trained somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So the three or four were people trained by Captain Dragan? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose so. And then they returned as instructors, as trainers, to the territory of Brcko, to the district of Brcko. But I can't remember any of their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness, in fact the Bosnian Serbs were preparing for the takeover of Brcko before the bridges were taken, were blown up, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't put it that way. I know that the Bosnian Serbs within the boundaries of their capabilities were preparing themselves for defence. I wouldn't be able to say anything about the takeover of Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, yesterday, you testified that -- and correct me if my understanding of your evidence is incorrect, but you testified you didn't see any JNA officers or men on the front lines, and you were unable to illuminate the issue of the JNA participation in a war in Brcko any further than that.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I adhere by my statement. I can't remember having seen a single JNA officer on the front line while I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: But it is a fact, isn't it, Mr. Maricic, that the JNA was cooperating with the paramilitary units that had arrived in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. I believe this to be true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, can you -- let me show you, Witness, then a document that's found in tab 7. Actually, let's go back -- let us go back to tab 4, Witness. And I would like to direct your attention, Witness, to page -- page 17 of the B/C/S. It's with the counter number 02:50:29. Your Honours, that's found on page 19. And Mr. Blagojevic, in the interview that was given, you didn't hear him say this but this is the transcript from that interview, text of it, he says -- the TV host says: "When you look at the photographs of our volunteers, they're all young men who have been killed. Here is Zeljko Markanovic, born in 1969, Bozo Pantic born 1952 he was born around 1956, Branislav Filipovic born in 1960, the oldest of them". Now, I want to ask you about one of the volunteers by the name of Branislav Filipovic. Did you know him or know about him?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've never heard of this name. The name doesn't ring a bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you ever hear the name Sumar?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was that one of the nicknames of a volunteer who came to Brcko to assist the Serbs at the beginning the war?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And Sumar was killed in Brcko, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Let's take a look, then, Witness, if we could turn to it tab 7 of this -- this needs a new number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: At that will be P1127.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Witness, this is a document that is dated the 7th of May in Brcko. It's pursuant to a decision by the Brcko -- by the War Presidency of the Brcko municipality, and it is a pass that is issued to Branislav Filipovic, and it is noted that he is a volunteer from Bijeljina and has War Presidency, Brcko municipality, with his signature. And then on the back of the document it has two names, Djordje Ristanic and Pero Markovic. So who is Pero Markovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do we have the original for the witness to look at, please? I think it might help him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I don't have the original with me in court, no, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why not, as might -- what I would respectfully ask my learned friend through Your Honour. It would clearly help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It would certainly help, Mr. Josse if it would be there. At the same time, "why not." I think that question was never asked of the Defence when it came to documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I'll withdraw the use of those words. I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The words came out of my mouth in an unfortunate manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what happens --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I accept that, and all my remarks should be addressed through Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Not directly to my learned friend. I apologise to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand, Mr. Josse, things that it would assist if we would have the original here. The copy is not -- not very clear, Mr. Harmon. That's one thing for certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't want to belabour this point. I will get a copy of the original here if this witness is having difficulty but I haven't heard this witness saying he's having difficulty when reading this document but if it's necessary I'll be more than happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, I can understand when the present document that Mr. Josse anticipated such a situation. Can you sufficiently see what it is? If not, we'll try to get the original at least. Mr. Maricic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It doesn't mean anything to me these signatures which are not clear. This is all unclear to me. I don't know who -- whose signatures these actually are. I'm familiar with the names but not with the signatures. This is -- this is not clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I must say that the one thing I can see here more or less well are the signatures rather than anything else, but you say you don't recognise those signatures.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm no the process of trying to get original now, Your Honour. I'll pass on this document for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, then, for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let's turn to tab 8, Witness. This is a document -- this is P529, tab 102. Witness, if you turn to that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, I'm going to turn to a different exhibit rather than tab 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness, let me turn to a document that is found at tab 11. This needs a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1128, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This, Witness, is an authorisation which permits Branislav Filipovic to bring munitions from Belgrade to the Brcko garrison for the needs of the garrisons in Brcko and Bosanski Samac, and then it describes the types of munitions as well as -- and it is signed for the garrison command in Brcko, Lieutenant Colonel Predrag Manojlovic. So this document confirms, does it not, Witness, that the paramilitaries were working with the JNA command in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no comment on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, let me turn to another document, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take that answer for you not being aware of such a thing or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know almost nothing about paramilitary units, especially not about the shipment of any arms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to return to this. Hopefully the original of that other document will be coming very shortly, so I'll just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Very, very shortly, I hope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And meanwhile?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And meanwhile I'll continue, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So let me turn to a different document, Witness. Are you aware, Mr. Maricic, that the paramilitaries who were operating in Brcko municipality were committing crimes against the Muslim and the Croat civilian populations?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally did not witness a single crime, but a lot of things happened there, and somebody must have done them. But who exactly I can't say. The crimes that are the subject of a lot of talk mainly happened while I was away for treatment or at the very beginning when I was on the front line. I told you that when I was on the front line I came home only once to wash and walk through town once and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In the 14 years since the start of the war in Brcko, Mr. Maricic, did you hear or receive any information that paramilitary formations who operated with the JNA and with the Crisis Staff and the War Presidency, those people, I'm talking about Mr. Blagojevic's men, Captain Dragan's men, Arkan's men, Mauzer's men, committed any crimes against the Muslim or Croat civilian population in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard all those stories, but I want to add that when the war began in Brcko the Crisis Staff and the civilian Presidency that was elected had no powers at all. They were only obliged to act as some sort of logistical organ to provide for the supply of flour and all the other necessities. They were not asked about anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When did you hear those stories?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I move around a lot, and when I came back from treatment I heard a lot about those events, and over the past 14 years I heard a lot about all that happened, especially about the Luka prison. But it's all what I heard from other people. I understood that I'm supposed to testify only about my direct knowledge. I don't know who perpetrated specific murders and killings apart from a couple of incidents in Luka. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let's start with Luka. What did you hear about Luka?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Luka did not even exist while I was on the battlefield in Brcko. It did not exist as a collection centre. And when I came back, it was already closed down. However, I heard a lot about it later, primarily from Kole who used to be the commander of Luka, and we lived in the same building. I also attended the recent trial against this Kole, who was convicted to six years in prison, and I also heard about it from other people because I live in a Serb neighbourhood. Luka is not far away, and I was able to learn about it from my neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In 1992, Mr. Maricic, what did you learn about Luka camp and the crimes that were committed in Luka camp?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992? Nothing, absolutely nothing. I didn't even know Luka existed then. I only learnt and even that later about Batkovic prison. I wasn't interested. I mean, I didn't even know it existed so as to be able to take an interest. I learned about it much later. Otherwise, I think I'm well-informed about the goings-on in Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I'm looking at the clock. We have several reasons we have to stop at a quarter to two. I would have one question for the witness and, once the witness has left the courtroom, I would like to inquire into how we will proceed and what progress we are making. Mr. Maricic, I would have one question, similar -- couple of sub-questions. Mr. Pero Markovic, was he an SDS member?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zarko Kozic, was he an SDS member.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Cosic. Cosic you mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Sinisa Kisic, same question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no one's a Communist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Simo Kojic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was an SDS member.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Miodrag Pajic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Radoslav Bogicevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he joined later and he was an SDS member, although only on paper, not in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said he joined later. What did he join later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You were asking about Bogicevic; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you said, "I think he joined later, and he was an SDS member, although only on paper, not in fact." What did he join later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean he joined the SDS a bit later. His brother was in the Socialist Party, and he became a senior manager later, so he joined the SDS in order to facilitate this appointment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This explanation you gave last is difficult to understand. If I read again your previous answer which said, "I think he joined later and he was an SDS member, although only on paper, not in fact." That sounds as if he joined not the SDS but another group, body, whatever. So could you tell me --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I don't accept that interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But accepted you -- object against it, I do understand. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's obviously a matter of translation. I don't read that in English in the way Your Honour has just interpreted it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. What we'll do that is check that both in B/C/S and in -- we'll then carefully look at it both in B/C/S, how the question reached the witness and also literally on how he answered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll do that before tomorrow afternoon. If Mr. -- I see that you're conferring with your case manager. Does that bring any -- shed any new light on -- perhaps not in the presence of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Precisely. Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Maricic, we have not finished with you yet. We'd like to see you back tomorrow, not in the morning but in the afternoon, a quarter past two. I again instruct you not to speak with anyone on the testimony you have given already and you're still about to give. Could you please follow Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So far as that's concerned, Mr. Karganovic understood the answer to be, yes, he was a member of the SDS. He wasn't very active.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But if Your Honour wants to check that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to have that checked because you understand the interpretation of this member and also the credibility and reliability of the witness might -- it might -- it might shed some light on it, either in a positive or in a negative way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If there is any prospect of having an answer to that before we resume tomorrow, the parties would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Harmon, how much time would you still think you'd still need? I'm not saying how much time you'll get but --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Less than one session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Less than one session. We'll consider how much time would be available to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Not much time, Your Honour. I'd say 30 to 45 minutes at the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll consider that. We will adjourn and resume tomorrow afternoon, quarter past two, same courtroom. Yes, Mr. Josse I see that. Before it's become effective..

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, very briefly. The issue of the documents that was mentioned earlier, there's been a lot of discussion in the intervening period. The order that the Chamber made regarding the re-numbering of P64A. I know both my learned friend, Mr. Harmon, and I have no objection to that being carried out forthwith and I know from Mr. Haider that would very much suit the Registry. So I would urge Your Honours to effectively ask that be done immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's good to have this answer so quickly. Yesterday, I think I invited you to come with any objections against Poplasen, et cetera, et cetera. We'll leave that tomorrow because we find no time to do it today.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The news for the witness who is due to arrive on Friday is extremely bad. I'll relay the rest of the information through one of Your Honour's legal officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Always with a copy to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I was going to do it orally but Mr. Harmon can listen to what I say to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I had a meeting starting at 1.46 p.m., so I'd like to go to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Orally to the legal officer, not orally to Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Fine. If -- the only thing of importance is that this kind of information is always very transparent. Yes. We will adjourn until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 23rd day of March, 2006, 2.15 p.m. 25
